findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case/whitespace sensitive and bypassable
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` compares the raw submitted email with exact string equality. There is no normalization in the new validator or in the User email assignment path, so on a case-sensitive database (Discourse uses PostgreSQL) a blocked address like `spam@example.com` can be submitted as `Spam@example.com` (or with surrounding whitespace) and will not match. The account is then allowed despite the block. Normalize the value before lookup and when storing block records, e.g. strip/downcase consistently and query with the normalized form.

findings.title: Validation has write side effects and double-counts blocked matches
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is a predicate but performs a read-modify-write on `match_count` and saves the record every time it is called. It is called from a model validator, so ordinary `user.valid?` checks mutate the blocklist table. This is especially visible in `UsersController#create`, which calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`: a blocked signup increments `match_count` twice for one attempt. The non-atomic `record.match_count += 1; record.save` also loses increments under concurrent requests. As a result, `match_count`/`last_match_at` are not reliable, and validation requests cause unnecessary writes. Move the statistics update out of the validator or make it an atomic, once-per-actual-attempt operation.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and bypassable
findings.body: The domain restriction regexp is built without an end anchor. With a whitelist setting of `example.com`, it compiles to `@(example\.com)`, which also matches the prefix of `user@example.com.evil.com`; that address is therefore accepted even though its domain is not whitelisted. Conversely, a blacklist can overblock unrelated hosts. Anchor the match to the actual domain boundary (or parse the domain and compare exact values) instead of using an unanchored substring regexp.

findings.title: Tests stub out the critical block lookup and never cover User validation
findings.body: Both new validator examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so they do not exercise the real database lookup, email normalization, or the `User` validation path. There is also no spec asserting that a `User` with a blocked or mixed-case blocked email is invalid, and no coverage for the whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved from `User` into this validator. These gaps are exactly what would catch the blocklist bypass and the unanchored domain regex. Add model/integration specs using real `BlockedEmail` records and a `User`/`valid?` path.
